subject: The World Around Us
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 8 periods = 320 minutes
Total: 8 periods · 5h 20min

periods.activity_title: From Trees to Paper — Tracing the Story
periods.textbook_anchor: How Paper is Made — Discuss whether we waste paper and how we can reduce that wastage (p. 122)

time_bands.activity: The teacher holds up common items — a drawing book, newspaper, and tissue — and asks children where they think these came from. Students share ideas freely, building a first spoken sense of paper's origin from natural materials.

Students open Textbook p. 119 and read the story of Pihu together. The class traces the journey: tree → wood pulp → paper, noting that making paper uses large numbers of trees, water, and energy. The teacher lists these three inputs on the board as students name them.

The teacher introduces the historical angle from the section: cloth, leaves, wooden boards, and palm leaves (talapatra) were used for writing in India long before wood-pulp paper existed. Children discuss which of these they have seen or heard about at home or from elders, making personal connections to the content.

Class discusses Textbook p. 122 questions — Do we waste paper? How could that be reduced? Students voice two or three concrete ideas. The teacher closes by naming the thread the class has built: paper comes from nature, and knowing that shapes how we use it.

periods.implied_lo: Students can trace how a manufactured everyday material originates from natural resources and explain the environmental cost of that production.
periods.section_context: Paper made from wood pulp; drawing books, newspapers, paper napkins, chart paper; trees, water, energy as inputs; historical writing materials — cloth, leaves, wooden boards, palm leaves (talapatra); banana fibre as alternative; paper wastage discussion.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask children if any grandparent or elder has told them about writing on leaves or slates — draw out that connection naturally before introducing talapatra. Keep the pace unhurried on the historical thread; children need time to connect traditional practice to natural materials.

periods.activity_title: Making Recycled Paper from Old Newspapers
periods.textbook_anchor: How Paper is Made — Make recycled paper using old newspapers, fenugreek seeds, and water by soaking, blending into pulp, rolling into thin sheets, and drying (p. 119)
materials: Old newspaper pieces (pre-torn, soaked overnight in water by the teacher as preparation)
piece of thin cloth or mesh

time_bands.activity: The teacher shows children the soaked newspaper-and-fenugreek mixture prepared beforehand and briefly explains the process visible on Textbook p. 119: soak → mash → spread → dry. Students predict what the fenugreek seeds might be doing in the mixture.

Working in groups, students mash and blend the soaked mixture by hand to form a smooth pulp, then spread the paste onto a flat base through the cloth or mesh and roll it carefully into a thin, even sheet. The teacher circulates, helping groups achieve an even thickness without tearing.
Sheets are set on a flat surface to begin drying. Students observe the wet sheet and describe its texture and colour in their notebooks, predicting how it will look and feel once dry.

Groups share one observation each about the process — what was hard, what surprised them. The teacher draws out the connection: the same basic steps (pulp → sheet → dry) happen at an industrial scale in paper mills, just with wood instead of newspaper.

periods.implied_lo: Students can follow a multi-step process to transform raw material into a new product, recording observations at each stage.
periods.section_context: Recycled paper making; old newspapers, fenugreek seeds, water as materials; soaking, grinding/mashing into pulp, rolling into thin sheets, drying as steps.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: The soaking step must be prepared by the teacher before the unit so the pulp is workable within the time available. Prompt groups to use equal amounts of mixture for a fair comparison of sheet thickness.

periods.activity_title: Natural Colour Experiment on Recycled Paper
periods.textbook_anchor: How Paper is Made — Colour pieces of recycled paper using natural ingredients in equal quantities and record observations in the table (p. 120)
materials: Small pieces of plain white drawing paper (as proxy for dried recycled paper, same size for each group)
natural colouring ingredients: beetroot juice, turmeric powder, spinach leaf paste, rose petals soaked in water, coffee powder solution

time_bands.activity: Students open Textbook p. 120. The teacher introduces the idea of natural dyes — colours obtained from plant parts (leaf, flower, root, seed, stem) — used traditionally to colour cloth and pots as well as paper. Children name any plant-based colour they know from home.

Each group receives identical pieces of paper and five natural colour solutions. Using equal amounts of each ingredient (same number of drops or same-size cotton swab), students apply one colour per paper piece, wait briefly, and observe. They record the colour produced and brightness for each ingredient in the observation table, noting which ingredients gave strong or faint colour.

Groups compare results across the class, noting which natural ingredient gave the brightest colour and which gave the faintest. The teacher asks: why is it important to use the same quantity of each ingredient? Students articulate the idea of a fair test.

Quick class share: students name one natural dye they would choose if making a greeting card and explain why. The teacher connects this to traditional craftspeople who select plant dyes deliberately for their properties.

periods.implied_lo: Students can conduct a simple controlled comparison, keeping one variable constant and recording differences in outcome across tested materials.
periods.section_context: Natural dyes from plant parts — leaf, flower, root, seed, stem; beetroot juice, turmeric, spinach, rose petals, coffee as test ingredients; same-size paper pieces; equal quantities; observation table recording colour and brightness.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask children whether they have seen their family use turmeric or flowers to colour food or fabric — this opens the cultural thread of natural dyes without labelling it. Emphasise that equal quantity is the control condition; let students discover that unevenness makes comparison impossible.

periods.activity_title: Create a Greeting Card or Paper Mask from Recycled Paper
periods.textbook_anchor: How Paper is Made — Make a greeting card, paper mask, or similar item from recycled paper (p. 121)
materials: Dried or semi-dried recycled paper sheets from the earlier paper-making unit (or plain newsprint as substitute)
any remaining natural dye from the colour experiment

time_bands.activity: Students look at Textbook p. 121 together. The teacher shows a simple greeting card folded from newsprint as an example, then opens the choice: children may make a greeting card, a paper mask, or another item they can think of using the recycled paper available.

Students design and create their chosen item, decorating with crayons or natural dye if available. The teacher circulates, encouraging children to think about the message or purpose of their item — who it is for, what it celebrates — making the creation purposeful rather than purely decorative.

A brief gallery walk: students place finished items on their desks and walk around quietly to see each other's work. Each student sticks a small sticky-note comment (or says one aloud) on a classmate's item — one thing they notice.

The teacher connects the activity back to the section's content: every item the class made came from a material that would otherwise have been waste. Children name the raw material their item started as: old newspaper.

periods.implied_lo: Students can transform discarded materials into a purposeful created object, demonstrating that waste materials have continued creative value.
periods.section_context: Greeting card, paper mask, or creative item made from recycled paper; old newspaper as raw material; natural dye for decoration.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Invite children who finish early to add a written message or a small natural-dye border to their item. The gallery walk should be unhurried and quiet so every child has time to take in several pieces.

periods.textbook_anchor: Making Responsible Choices — Discuss the situations in the table and identify which of the 5Rs each belongs to (p. 125)

time_bands.activity: The teacher writes the five Rs on the board — Refuse, Reduce, Reuse, Repurpose, Recycle — and asks the class to guess what each might mean before reading any definition. Students suggest meanings from the words alone, building a first intuitive map.

Students open Textbook p. 125. The class reads each situation in the table aloud — Maya refusing a plastic straw, Rohan using blank pages of an old notebook, Sara giving old books to younger students, Kabir painting an old bottle as a flower vase, Priya cutting old clothes to make a bag, a shopkeeper folding newspapers into envelopes. In pairs, students discuss and write down which R each situation belongs to.

Pairs share their answers. The teacher facilitates whole-class discussion where there is disagreement — for example, whether repurposing and reusing can overlap — encouraging children to justify their reasoning rather than simply accept the teacher's answer.

Students write one sentence in their notebook: a situation from their own daily life and which R it belongs to. Two or three children share. The teacher affirms that each small choice adds up across many people.

periods.implied_lo: Students can classify real-life resource-use behaviours into a named framework of conservation practices and justify their classification with reasoning.
periods.section_context: 5Rs — Refuse, Reduce, Reuse, Repurpose, Recycle; situations: refusing a paper cup, using both sides of paper, giving old books to younger students, painting an old bottle as a vase, cutting old clothes into a bag, folding newspapers into envelopes; Braille as a specialised paper use.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask whether anyone in their family already does one of these things without calling it a 'rule' — this connects the formal framework to existing household practice. Let pairs disagree for a moment before opening to the class; productive uncertainty deepens classification thinking.

periods.activity_title: Turning Old Paper into a Toy or Decoration
periods.section_ref: Let Us Get Creative with Paper
periods.textbook_anchor: How Paper is Made — Make a greeting card, paper mask, or similar item from recycled paper (p. 121)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook figures of newspaper figures, paper fans, and decorative birds

time_bands.activity: The teacher shows the textbook examples of a newspaper figure, a paper fan, and a decorative bird, asking: what do all of these have in common as a starting material? Students recognise old paper as the shared ingredient and connect this to Repurpose from the 5Rs framework the class has already built.

Each student chooses one item to make — a paper fan, a rolled-newspaper figure, a decorative bird, or their own invention — using only old newspaper and scrap paper available on the desk. The teacher encourages inventive choices and circulates to support folding or rolling techniques without directing the design.

Students write one sentence below or beside their item (on a scrap-paper label): what their item is, what material it is made from, and what they could use it for. This connects creation to purposeful use, reinforcing the Repurpose principle.

The teacher collects or displays items briefly and asks: did anyone invent something not shown in the textbook? Those children name their invention. The class notes that creative use of waste paper is an open-ended activity — the examples are a starting point, not a complete list.

periods.implied_lo: Students can apply the principle of repurposing to produce a new functional or decorative object from discarded paper, demonstrating creative problem-solving with waste material.
periods.section_context: Old newspaper and scrap paper transformed into toys and decorative items; examples — newspaper figures, paper fans, decorative birds; student-invented items; Repurpose as the animating 5R principle.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Prompt children who are unsure where to start by asking: what shape does this paper make naturally when you fold it? Allowing free invention alongside the textbook examples surfaces richer responses and keeps the activity genuinely creative.

periods.activity_title: Reflecting on Our Paper Choices — Writing Our 5Rs Commitments
periods.textbook_anchor: Let us reflect — Write one step you can take for each of the 5Rs in the boxes given (p. 127)

time_bands.activity: Students open Textbook p. 127 and read the first reflection question together: What objects can be made from paper pulp? Children brainstorm answers aloud, drawing on the paper-making and creative-paper content the class has worked through. The teacher notes responses on the board.

Students add to the board list by asking teachers or each other for ideas not already mentioned, practising the textbook's suggestion to consult elders and teachers. Children note two or three ideas in their own notebooks (Textbook p. 127, first reflection).

Students work individually on Textbook p. 127's second reflection: writing one specific, personal step they will take for each of the five Rs. The teacher walks quietly and asks individuals to say their step aloud softly before writing, helping them move from vague intent to a concrete action.

Pairs share their written steps, choosing one they feel most confident they can actually do. The class then hears five volunteers — one per R — read their step. The teacher connects each step to the broader idea: small personal changes, multiplied across many people, protect trees and reduce pollution.

Students fold their notebook open to the 5Rs page and place it on the desk for a moment, reading what they wrote silently. The teacher closes by noting that returning to this page after some time is a way to check whether their intention became a habit.

periods.implied_lo: Students can translate an environmental framework into specific, personally committed actions for their own daily life, explaining how each action connects to resource conservation.
periods.section_context: Objects makeable from paper pulp; personal 5Rs action steps — one step per R: Refuse, Reduce, Reuse, Repurpose, Recycle; daily changes to avoid paper wastage; discussion of paper-use changes at individual level.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Encourage children to name an action they genuinely think they will do, not the most impressive one — this keeps the reflection honest rather than performative. Ask: have any of you already been doing one of these without knowing it had a name?

periods.activity_title: Observing and Classifying Different Types of Paper
periods.section_ref: Different Types of Paper and their Uses
periods.textbook_anchor: Different Types of Paper and their Uses — Observe different types of paper used in daily life, paste small pieces in the space provided, and write their uses (p. 123)
materials: Small pieces of writing paper, newspaper, art paper, cardboard, and tissue paper (one set per student or pair)

time_bands.activity: The teacher places one piece of each paper type on a shared surface — writing paper, newspaper, art paper, cardboard, tissue. Students handle each in turn without being told the name, describing what they feel: thick or thin, rough or smooth, stiff or floppy, absorbent or not. Observations are spoken aloud and listed on the board.

Students open Textbook p. 123 and follow the activity: they paste a small piece of each paper type in the space provided and write one or two uses for that type. The teacher circulates, prompting children to link the property they felt to the use — for example, tissue is soft and absorbent, so it is used for wiping; cardboard is thick and stiff, so it is used for boxes.

Students examine their completed table and answer two questions in their notebooks: Which paper type uses the most trees to produce, and why? Which paper type would they choose for wrapping a fragile gift, and why? These require connecting observed property to reasoning about natural resource use and purpose.

A short class share: students give one property-to-use match they found most surprising. The teacher closes by connecting paper properties back to the chapter's opening thread — every paper type begins in natural materials, and knowing what each type needs helps us choose more responsibly.

periods.implied_lo: Students can observe and record the physical properties of different materials, then connect those properties to the specific uses that make each material suited to a human purpose.
periods.section_context: Writing paper, newspaper, art paper, cardboard, tissue paper; properties — thin, soft, absorbent, thick, hard, stiff; uses — writing, news printing, art, packaging boxes, wiping; property-to-use reasoning.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Let students handle the samples before naming them — property observation should precede labelling. Ask: if cardboard were soft, could it protect objects in a box? This kind of counterfactual question makes the property-to-use link explicit.

assessment_items.question_text: Paper that we use every day is made mainly from which natural resource?
assessment_items.annotation: Correct answer is A. This is a direct recall check on the chapter's opening content. A student selecting B, C, or D has not engaged with the paper-origin discussion.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can trace how a manufactured everyday material originates from natural resources and explain the environmental cost of that production.

competency.competency_text: Describes usage of natural resources in their immediate environment

what_each_option_reveals.B: Confuses the raw material for glass or cement with that of paper; suggests the student did not engage with the paper-origin content.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Confuses paper's origin with that of metals; indicates a broad confusion between manufactured materials and their sources.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Confuses paper with pottery or brick-making; suggests the student linked 'made from the ground' but selected a non-wood material.

assessment_items.question_text: A student made recycled paper using old newspaper, fenugreek seeds, and water. Write the steps she followed in the correct order.
expected_elements: Tear old newspaper into pieces and soak them together with fenugreek seeds in water (overnight or for some time).
Mash or grind the soaked mixture to form a smooth pulp.
Spread the pulp onto a flat surface and roll it into a thin, even sheet.
assessment_items.annotation: Award one mark per correctly stated step in a logical sequence. Accept reasonable variation in wording. All four steps must be present for full credit; partial credit for three correct steps in order.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can follow a multi-step process to transform raw material into a new product, recording observations at each stage.

competency.competency_text: Uses local materials to create simple objects (family tree, envelopes, origami animals) on their own for display or use in classroom processes

expected_elements: Soaking torn newspaper pieces with fenugreek seeds in water.
Mashing or grinding the soaked mixture into pulp.
Spreading the pulp flat and rolling into a thin sheet.

assessment_items.question_text: In the natural colour experiment, Riya used different amounts of beetroot juice and turmeric on her paper pieces. Her classmate said the experiment was not fair. Why did the classmate say this? What should Riya do to make it fair?
expected_elements: The experiment was not fair because using different amounts of each colour ingredient means you cannot tell whether colour differences are due to the ingredient itself or due to the amount used.
To make it fair, Riya should use the same quantity (same number of drops or same-sized amount) of every natural ingredient on each paper piece.
assessment_items.annotation: Full credit requires both elements: identifying unequal quantity as the problem AND stating that equal quantities are the fix. Partial credit for identifying the problem without stating the correction.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can conduct a simple controlled comparison, keeping one variable constant and recording differences in outcome across tested materials.

competency.competency_text: Performs simple inquiry related to specific questions independently or in groups

expected_elements: Explanation that unequal quantities mean differences in colour could be due to amount, not the ingredient itself — making comparison invalid.
Correction: use the same quantity of each ingredient so that the only difference between pieces is the type of natural dye.

assessment_items.task: Think of someone you would like to give a gift to — a friend, a family member, or a teacher. Using only old newspaper or scrap paper available in your classroom, make a greeting card or a small decorative item for that person. On the back of your item or on a separate scrap piece, write: (1) what your item is, (2) who it is for, and (3) why you chose to make it from waste paper instead of buying new paper.
assessment_items.scaffold:
My item is: ___
It is for: ___
I made it from waste paper because: ___
format_of_output: A physical greeting card or decorative item made from old newspaper or scrap paper
A short written label on the back with the three prompted answers
assessment_items.annotation: Assess both the physical item and the written label. The item need not be elaborate; the key indicator is that it was made from discarded paper. The written label should show a genuine reason connected to resource conservation, not simply 'because the teacher said so'.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can transform discarded materials into a purposeful created object, demonstrating that waste materials have continued creative value.

competency.competency_text: Uses local materials to create simple objects (family tree, envelopes, origami animals) on their own for display or use in classroom processes

OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: Whether the student can purposefully re-use waste paper to create something with intended meaning, and articulate the conservation reasoning behind that choice.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: The three-part label checks: identification of the created item, social purposefulness (it is for someone), and environmental reasoning (why waste paper rather than new paper). All three should be present.
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong: item is clearly crafted with intention; label names the recipient personally and gives a conservation reason such as 'to save trees' or 'so this paper is not thrown away'. Weak: item is a torn, unformed scrap; label is blank or says only 'I was told to'.
OPEN_TASK.inclusivity: Children who have difficulty with fine-motor folding can tear and paste shapes instead. The written label can be dictated to the teacher and transcribed if a child has writing difficulty.
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: The task mirrors the textbook activity and tests creative application with real material — a text-only response cannot demonstrate the competency.

assessment_items.question_text: Kabir painted an old glass bottle and put flowers in it. Which of the 5Rs does his action belong to?
assessment_items.annotation: Correct answer is B. Repurpose means giving an old item a new use without breaking it down; Kabir gave the bottle a new function as a vase. This item was drawn directly from the classification activity in the textbook.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can classify real-life resource-use behaviours into a named framework of conservation practices and justify their classification with reasoning.

competency.competency_text: Demonstrates how natural resources can be shared, maintained, and conserved (trees, use of rainwater, benefits of millets)

what_each_option_reveals.A: Confuses repurposing with recycling; the student may think any reuse of an old object is recycling, missing that recycling involves breaking the material down.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Confuses repurposing with refusing; the student may not have a clear definition of Refuse as declining to accept/use something in the first place.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Confuses repurposing with reducing; the student may be conflating 'using less' with 'using differently'.

assessment_items.task: Using only old newspaper available on your desk, make one object of your choice — a toy, a decorative item, or something useful. When you have finished, write one sentence on a scrap piece of paper: what your object is and what someone could use it for.
assessment_items.scaffold:
My object is: ___
Someone could use it for: ___
format_of_output: A physical object made from old newspaper
A one-sentence written label naming the object and its use
assessment_items.annotation: The item must be made entirely from newspaper during the assessment sitting. The label should identify the object and propose a genuine use. Accept any creative invention; the criterion is intentional making with a stated purpose.
assessment_items.chapter_section: Let Us Get Creative with Paper
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can apply the principle of repurposing to produce a new functional or decorative object from discarded paper, demonstrating creative problem-solving with waste material.

competency.competency_text: Learns about basic social and behavioural norms, values, and dispositions that benefit our social and natural environments and that help our society function smoothly (using dustbins, standing in queues, conserving water, using public transportation, keeping one's environment clean, always helping others in need regardless of background)

OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: Whether the student can independently apply the repurpose principle by turning discarded paper into a new object with a purposeful use, within a single sitting.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: The label checks that the student can name what they made and articulate a use for it — connecting creative output to purposeful intent rather than random folding.
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong: a recognisable object (fan, figure, box, hat) with a plausible stated use. Weak: an unformed scrap with no label or a label that only repeats the task instruction.
OPEN_TASK.inclusivity: Students may choose any object type — there is no single correct answer. Children with fine-motor difficulty may tear and stack shapes rather than fold. The written label may be dictated.
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: The competency is demonstrated through making, not through describing making; a text-only response does not satisfy the implied_lo.

assessment_items.question_text: Priya wants to reduce the amount of paper she wastes at school. Using the 5Rs framework, write at least three specific actions she could take — one for any three of the five Rs — and explain how each action helps protect trees.
look_for: Three clearly named R labels (from Refuse, Reduce, Reuse, Repurpose, Recycle) with one action each.
Each action is specific and practical — not a vague statement like 'use less paper' but a concrete step such as 'use both sides of notebook pages before buying a new one'.
Each action is linked to tree protection with a brief explanation — e.g. using less paper means fewer trees need to be cut.
Responses drawn from the student's own daily school experience, showing personal internalisation rather than copied text.
assessment_items.annotation: Full credit: three specific actions, three R labels correctly matched, three tree-protection explanations. Partial credit: two out of three complete combinations. Accept regionally varied examples (e.g. using both sides of a slate, giving old books to a sibling) as equally valid. Regional-variation note: accept any locally relevant paper-conservation practice the student names — correct answers are not limited to the textbook examples.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can translate an environmental framework into specific, personally committed actions for their own daily life, explaining how each action connects to resource conservation.

competency.competency_text: Demonstrates how natural resources can be shared, maintained, and conserved (trees, use of rainwater, benefits of millets)

look_for: Three R labels correctly identified from the five (Refuse, Reduce, Reuse, Repurpose, Recycle).
Each action is concrete and school-relevant, not a paraphrase of the definition.
Each explanation links the action to fewer trees being cut, less energy used, or less waste generated.
The student writes in first or third person consistently, showing personal ownership of the framework rather than mechanical listing.

assessment_items.question_text: Which property of tissue paper makes it most useful for wiping?

options.label: B
options.text: It is thin, soft, and absorbent.

assessment_items.annotation: Correct answer is B. The item tests whether the student can connect observed properties to a specific use, the core skill of the paper-classification activity. Options A, C, and D describe properties of other paper types observed in the same activity.
assessment_items.chapter_section: Different Types of Paper and their Uses
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can observe and record the physical properties of different materials, then connect those properties to the specific uses that make each material suited to a human purpose.

competency.competency_text: Describes usage of natural resources in their immediate environment

what_each_option_reveals.A: Describes cardboard properties applied to tissue; student may not have handled and differentiated the samples carefully during the observation activity.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Combines a property of cardboard (stiff) with a property tissue does not have (waterproof); suggests the student confused paper types during classification.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Describes properties of no paper type in the chapter; suggests the student guessed without drawing on observed properties.
